title: Live Chat API Primer — Streaming, Params, Retries & Console Tour
topics: Console walkthrough: latency, token cost, routes
Optimize suggestions: batching, KV/prefix caching, quantized fallbacks
summary: AE + SE ran a 42-minute primer for BlueSky Payments on Redwood's hosted Chat/Text generation API. Covered streaming mechanics, pragmatic param knobs, how to implement retries and idempotency, and a quick tour of the Console and Optimize suggestions. Customer asked about latency guarantees, VPC/dedicated options for PCI-sensitive flows, and an initial POC plan was sketched.

transcript:
Meeting start: 2026-10-06 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42m
Attendees: Maria (Redwood AE), Kevin (Redwood SE), Samir (BlueSky ML), Priya (BlueSky CTO), Liam (PM)

[00:00] Maria: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maria from Redwood, AE on the account. Kevin is our solutions engineer, he'll take the demo bits. Quick agenda — high level chat API, streaming behaviors, params you should tune, retry/backoff patterns, and a Console tour showing latency and cost.

[00:18] Samir: Cool, quick context — we are building an in-app support assistant and transaction summarizer. PCI scope is a concern, so we want to explore hosted first but need to understand dedicated / VPC options. Latency target 200-300ms for short utterances, but we have bursts up to 120 QPS during peak.

[00:36] Kevin: Great. We'll show hosted flow that most customers start with; then we'll call out dedicated for isolation. First, streaming — Redwood streams tokens as they're generated over SSE/websocket style streams. You can render partial tokens to the UI. That lowers perceived latency vs waiting for full response.

[01:10] Liam: Is streaming chunk size configurable? We worry about jitter in UI.

[01:25] Kevin: Good question. The runtime emits small deltas; on our SDKs you can buffer client-side and flush every N ms or after X tokens. Console shows typical distribution, and Optimize will recommend batching windows given your QPS to keep costs down.

[02:02] Priya: If a stream fails mid-response, what's best practice? We have flaky mobile clients.

[02:18] Kevin: Two options — client-side resume with idempotency keys, or server-side fallback. We recommend an idempotency token per user-turn so you can safely retry a request; on 429s we do exponential backoff with jitter. For mid-stream disconnects you can re-hydrate conversation state + KV cache, and request from the last confirmed token index. Note: some smaller model variants have different cache semantics — we sometimes see the term K-V cache transcribed as K V cache in logs, so your client should store conversation IDs not raw KV blobs.

[03:05] Samir: Hmm, the idempotency flow — is that baked into SDKs?

[03:15] Maria: Yes, our SDK has idempotency helper headers. There's also a server side idempotency store if you want Redwood to handle retries automatically for certain routes. We'll link the SDK snippet.

[03:40] Kevin: Next, params. Temperature and top_p control creativity — for deterministic outputs we generally set temperature 0 to 0.2, top_p 0.8-0.95. Max_tokens you should cap to expected reply size; console will surface token histograms so you can tune. We also recommend response_format constraints and structured output with function calls if you need JSON shapes.

[04:45] Liam: Can we stream function call tokens? We need partial JSON to start rendering.

[04:58] Kevin: Yes, function call payloads stream too. Be careful with partial JSON — use a streaming-merge step client-side. Also set a fairly small chunk timeout to avoid long stalls.

[05:32] Priya: Are there latency vs cost tradeoffs? If we want 200ms p95 do we need more expensive model types or dedicated pools?

[05:48] Kevin: Right. Short answer, yes: lower-latency SLOs often map to dedicated or pinned capacity and smaller sequence-length optimized kernels. Our Console has a latency vs cost view — you can compare model variants and quantization profiles. Optimize can recommend a quantized variant that saves ~30-50% on tokens while keeping quality. For sub-200ms p95 you often run smaller context models with dedicated GPUs or optimized pinned slices.

[06:35] Samir: For PCI data we probably need private or dedicated. What's the fastest path to validate?

[06:48] Maria: Typically start hosted with token redaction for PII and use dedicated when you need strict isolation. We can arrange a Private deployment conversation if you expect regulatory constraints; I'll share the VPC checklist and SOC2 docs.

[07:10] Kevin: Demo time — I'm going to share my screen. Starting with a simple chat call from the SDK (Node).

[07:28] Kevin: Code snippet: createConversation -> sendMessage({stream: true, idempotencyKey: uuid}) -> subscribe to response events. Here you can see the onDelta handler gets partial text chunks. Note there's a small mis- transcribe in the snippet — we accidentally refer to prefix-cache as prefix-cash in the comment, ignore that.

[08:12] Kevin: Live test — sending a short system+user prompt: 'Summarize last transaction for user 1457 in two lines.'

[08:28] [live stream output audio] Kevin: (demo) streaming: 'Transaction on 2026-10-01 — charge $23.45 to card ending ...' — partial appears in UI at 110ms after first token.

[09:05] Samir: That's pretty snappy for an example. What's the token usage?

[09:12] Kevin: Console reports about 28 request tokens and 14 response tokens, total 42. For pricing we'll show per-1k request/response token rates; Optimize also recommends caching common prefixes like 'Summarize last transaction' to shave requests.

[09:45] Liam: About retries — do you recommend client or server retry logic? And how to handle duplicate actions (e.g., refund triggers)?

[09:57] Kevin: For idempotent read-only operations, client retries with idempotency keys + exponential backoff are fine. For actions that mutate state you should implement at-least-once guarded by server-side idempotency or a confirmation step. Redwood also supports 'dry-run' mode responses for safety during UI flows.

[10:35] Priya: Any gotchas with streaming in mobile networks?

[10:45] Kevin: Mobile networks sometimes tear the socket; implement reconnect + resume. Also consider smaller chunk sizes and lower client-side buffer times. Use the SDK's auto-reconnect; we saw one customer note that streaming chunk order can be off when multiple parallel requests hit the same connection — don't multiplex unrelated conversations on a single socket.

[11:30] Maria: Quick Console tour — latency dashboard, per-route tokens, and the Optimize tab. You can see suggestions like: enable prefix caching, try quantized variant q4_0 for this workload, and set batching window 50ms for small bursts.

[12:05] Kevin: Note the Optimize suggestion also shows estimated cost delta and expected impact on latency. It's not perfect but gives a good starting point. You can accept a suggestion to auto-apply to a non-prod route.

[12:40] Samir: How do canary rollouts work if we want to test the quantized model?

[12:52] Kevin: We support weighted routing per model variant. You can route 10% traffic to quantized model, measure hallucination rate against eval prompts, and then increase. Console stores evals so you can compare metrics side-by-side.

[13:25] Liam: We have a separate question about backpressure — when our upstream queue fills, will Redwood slow responses or start rejecting?

[13:38] Kevin: Policy-based routing — you can choose to queue with a max latency SLO, reject with 429, or spill to a cheaper model. For enterprise customers we configure burst capacity and autoscaling thresholds.

[14:10] Priya: Security — SSO, audit logs, and key management?

[14:22] Maria: We support SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, RBAC per-team, and audit logs with export. For key management we integrate with KMS/HSM and can bring-your-own-keys for Private deployments. I'll include the SOC2 + encryption-at-rest whitepaper.

[15:05] Samir: Good. Do you have concrete numbers for p95 latency on hosted?

[15:18] Kevin: For hosted small-model gen on standard pool, p95 for short prompts is typically 200-400ms depending on seq len and load. We publish model perf profiles in the model catalog — the Console overlay will show real-time p95 by region. If we need <200ms steady p95, we recommend Dedicated pinned slices.

[16:00] Maria: Quick live failover demo — I'll trigger a synthetic 503 on the primary route.

[16:15] Kevin: You can see the fallback policy kicked in — traffic directed to variant 'gpt-like-small-fallback' within 250ms. Client saw a short reconnect and resumed streaming.

[16:40] Samir: Nice. For billing, are retransmitted tokens billed?

[16:50] Kevin: Retries that replay the request are billed the same as any request; Optimize suggests caching/prefix reuse to avoid repeated token generation. For streaming partial reconnects we do not charge for partial failed transmissions, but full retried requests are counted. We'll send the precise billing rules in the pricing deck.

[17:20] Priya: Any examples of customers reducing cost without harming quality?

[17:33] Kevin: Yes — a fintech customer used prefix caching + q4 quantized variant and reduced cost 42% while keeping eval pass rate within tolerance. We can share anonymized case study.

[18:00] Liam: For our POC, what's a realistic scope and timeline?

[18:12] Maria: Start with hosted trial, seed with 50 prompts, run bench tests for latency and token counts (1–2 weeks), then decide on Dedicated if isolation is required. POC scoping call should include infra (networking), security, and product. Proposed follow-up 2026-10-14.

[18:45] Samir: Sounds good. A couple of nitty gritty: do you support response streaming in Gradual JSON mode, and is there a max stream time?

[18:58] Kevin: We support streaming partial JSON but recommend a post-stream merge. Max stream duration is configurable per-route; default is 60s on hosted but can be tuned on Dedicated.

[19:25] (brief cross-talk)

[19:40] Maria: Quick recap — we'll send pricing, SOC2 docs, and the SDK snippet. Kevin will run the latency bench and Samir will share prompts. Any other blockers?

[20:00] Priya: One last ask — can Redwood sign an NDA and provide a data processing addendum?

[20:12] Maria: Yes, we have standard DPA and can do an NDA. I'll cc legal.

[20:30] Liam: Great. Also, do you have a recommended alerting threshold for token cost spikes?

[20:42] Kevin: We recommend alerting at 20% over expected monthly burn for the first month and 10% thereafter. Console supports budget alerts per project.

[21:05] Samir: Perfect. We'll send the prompt set and open the trial.

[21:18] Maria: Thank you all — we'll follow up with the deck and next-step calendar invite.

[21:30] Meeting end.

Note: transcription contains minor mis-hearings (e.g., prefix-cash vs prefix-cache), occasional speaker labels simplified.
